options.label: The preserved remains or traces of a living thing from long ago
options.feedback: Correct. A fossil is any preserved evidence of past life, from bones to footprints.

options.label: A rock that looks like an animal but was never alive
options.feedback: Incorrect. Fossilized remains come from actual living things, not from rocks that merely resemble them.

options.label: A modern animal that has hardened into stone
options.feedback: Incorrect. Fossils are from organisms that lived long ago, not from modern animals turning to stone.

options.label: A copy of an animal made by an artist
options.feedback: Incorrect. That is an artistic reproduction, not a fossil, which is natural and ancient.

items.ok_line: A fossil is preserved evidence of ancient life.
items.ko_line: Remember, fossils are real remains or traces, not modern or artificial.
items.exp_text: A fossil is the preserved remains or traces of an organism that lived in the past, such as bones, shells, footprints, or even droppings. This preservation happens naturally over millions of years.

items.prompt: In which type of rock are fossils almost always found?

options.label: Igneous rock, like cooled lava
options.feedback: Incorrect. Igneous rock forms from molten material and is too hot to preserve remains; fossils are rarely found there.

options.label: Sedimentary rock, like sandstone or shale
options.feedback: Correct. Sedimentary rock is made from layers of mud, sand, and other particles that can bury and preserve remains.

options.label: Metamorphic rock, like marble
options.feedback: Incorrect. Metamorphic rock forms under great heat and pressure, which would destroy or alter fossils.

options.label: Any rock type equally
options.feedback: Incorrect. Only sedimentary rock typically preserves fossils because it forms gently from deposited materials.

items.ko_line: Igneous and metamorphic rocks are too hot or pressured for fossils.
items.exp_text: Fossils are found in sedimentary rock, which forms from layers of sediment like mud and sand that settle and harden over time. These layers can bury organisms quickly and protect them from decay.

options.label: A hollow space left after the original organism decays
options.feedback: Correct. A mold is the empty impression or cavity in rock that shows the shape of the original organism.

options.label: A solid copy of the organism made of minerals
options.feedback: Incorrect. That describes a cast, which fills in a mold, not the mold itself.

options.label: An organism preserved whole in amber
options.feedback: Incorrect. Amber preserves the original organism, not a mold of it.

options.label: A footprint left in mud
options.feedback: Incorrect. A footprint is a trace fossil, but a mold specifically refers to an impression of a body part, not a track.

items.ok_line: A mold is the empty imprint of an organism.
items.ko_line: A mold is hollow; a cast is the filled copy.
items.exp_text: A fossil mold is a hollow impression left in rock after the original organism dissolved or decayed away. It preserves the external shape but not the material itself.

options.label: A fossilized egg
options.feedback: Incorrect. An egg fossil is an egg, not a coprolite, which is fossilized dung.

options.label: A fossilized shell
options.feedback: Incorrect. A shell is a body part, while a coprolite is a waste product.

options.label: A fossilized footprint
options.feedback: Incorrect. A footprint is a trace fossil of movement, not of digestion.

options.label: Fossilized animal dung
options.feedback: Correct. Coprolites are preserved droppings that can reveal what an animal ate.

items.ko_line: It's dung, not eggs, shells, or tracks.
items.exp_text: A coprolite is fossilized dung from an animal that lived long ago. It can contain plant fragments, bones, or other remnants that show what the animal consumed.

items.prompt: Why are fossils of bones more common than fossils of skin or muscle?

options.label: Bones are harder and decay more slowly than soft tissues
options.feedback: Correct. Hard parts like bones resist decay and are more likely to survive long enough to be buried and preserved.

options.label: Skin and muscle are never preserved in any form
options.feedback: Incorrect. Soft tissues can be preserved in special cases like amber or permafrost, though rarely.

options.label: Bones are buried more often because animals lived underground
options.feedback: Incorrect. Most animals did not live underground, but bones still decay slower when exposed.

options.label: Soft tissues turn into bone after death
options.feedback: Incorrect. Soft tissues decay or may be replaced by minerals, but they do not become bone.

items.ok_line: Bones decay slower than soft tissue.
items.ko_line: Hard parts are more likely to fossilize.
items.exp_text: Bones and teeth are made of hard minerals that resist decay, so they are more likely to be buried and preserved. Soft tissues like muscle and skin decompose quickly, so their fossils are rare.

options.label: The freezing of an animal in ice
options.feedback: Incorrect. Freezing preserves the original tissue, while permineralization involves minerals replacing the bone.

options.label: The gradual filling of bone pores with minerals from water
options.feedback: Correct. In permineralization, mineral-rich water seeps into bone and deposits minerals, turning it into stone.

options.label: The pressing of sediment into a footprint
options.feedback: Incorrect. That describes the formation of a trace fossil, not mineral replacement.

options.label: The escape of gas from decaying bodies
options.feedback: Incorrect. Gas release is part of decay, not fossilization.

items.ko_line: Minerals fill the bone's tiny spaces.
items.exp_text: Permineralization is a fossilization process where groundwater carrying dissolved minerals seeps into the pores of buried bone. The minerals crystallize and fill the spaces, making the bone hard as rock.

items.prompt: What kind of fossil is a dinosaur footprint?

options.label: A body fossil
options.feedback: Incorrect. A body fossil is part of the organism itself, like a bone, not a mark it left.

options.label: A mold fossil
options.feedback: Incorrect. A mold is an impression of a body part, not a track left by movement.

options.label: A trace fossil
options.feedback: Correct. Footprints, burrows, and nests are trace fossils, which record an animal's activity, not its body.

options.label: A coprolite
options.feedback: Incorrect. A coprolite is fossilized dung, not a footprint.

items.ko_line: It's a trace, not a whole body or droppings.
items.exp_text: A dinosaur footprint is a trace fossil because it preserves evidence of the animal's behavior, such as walking, rather than its physical remains. Trace fossils include tracks, burrows, and bite marks.

items.prompt: Why can amber preserve an insect with fine details?

options.label: Amber is very hard and crushes the insect into shape
options.feedback: Incorrect. Amber is sticky tree resin that flows around the insect, not something that crushes it.

options.label: Amber heats the insect and bakes it dry
options.feedback: Incorrect. Heat would damage the insect, not preserve it; resin preserves by sealing it out of the air.

options.label: Amber replaces the insect's body with stone
options.feedback: Incorrect. That is permineralization, not amber preservation; amber encases the original body.

options.label: Amber is sticky resin that seals the insect away from air and decay
options.feedback: Correct. Tree resin traps the insect and hardens, preventing decay and preserving even delicate parts.

items.ko_line: Resin covers, not crushes or replaces.
items.exp_text: Amber is fossilized tree resin. When an insect gets trapped in the sticky resin, it hardens and completely seals the insect from air and bacteria, stopping decay and preserving soft tissues like wings and hairs.

items.prompt: What does a frozen mammoth in permafrost most likely preserve that a bone fossil cannot?

options.label: Soft tissue like skin and hair
options.feedback: Correct. Freezing preserves original soft tissues, while fossilization usually only leaves hard parts.

options.label: The shape of its bones
options.feedback: Incorrect. That is preserved in fossils, but not the unique advantage of freezing.

options.label: Coprolites inside its stomach
options.feedback: Incorrect. While possible, the main difference is soft tissue, not just stomach contents.

options.label: A mold of its body
options.feedback: Incorrect. A mold is a rock impression, not preserved original tissue.

items.ko_line: Ice keeps soft parts, unlike fossilization.
items.exp_text: When a mammoth is frozen in permafrost, the cold stops decay, so skin, muscle, hair, and even internal organs can survive. Fossilization, in contrast, usually only preserves hard parts like bones.

items.prompt: What can the preserved skin texture on a fossil reveal?

options.label: What the animal ate
options.feedback: Incorrect. Diet is revealed by teeth or coprolites, not skin texture.

options.label: What the animal's outer covering looked like
options.feedback: Correct. Skin impressions show scales, feathers, or patterns that reveal the external appearance.

options.label: How fast the animal ran
options.feedback: Incorrect. Speed is inferred from bones and tracks, not skin texture.

options.label: Where the animal lived
options.feedback: Incorrect. Habitat is hinted by rock type, but skin texture doesn't show location.

items.ok_line: Skin texture shows what the outside looked like.
items.ko_line: Texture is about covering, not diet or speed.
items.exp_text: Fossilized skin impressions preserve the surface pattern of scales, feathers, or other coverings. This tells paleontologists what the animal looked like on the outside, even though the original skin is gone.
